content:
Hi everyone,
I'm a software engineer and an independent researcher, and I am fairly new to formalizing mathematics in Lean.
I recently saw Kim Morrison's elegant formalization of the odd-m cases for Knuth's Torus Decomposition problem. Keston Aquino-Michaels also recently closed the general even cases (m >= 8), which left the non-degenerate base cases of m=4 and m=6 wide open.
I just computationally closed both of these final cases. I used a custom incremental Simulated Annealing engine to find the arrays, and then ported the resulting witnesses into Lean 4 to formally verify the topological boundaries and the complete 216-step orbits. Because I am still an amateur with Lean, I relied heavily on the decide tactic, and the proofs compile in the trusted kernel with zero sorrys (though m=6 required bumping maxHeartbeats).
In the interest of full transparency, this work is part of a broader project exploring AI-assisted software engineering. I used an autonomous AI coding agent to help write the search engine and format the Lean proofs, though the final mathematical verification rests entirely on Lean's kernel.
The full manuscript PDF and the Lean proofs are available on my GitHub here:
https://github.com/bneb/perqed/blob/main/paper%2Ftorus_decomposition.pdf
I also wrote up a short blog post on the SA engineering and the incremental state caching here:
https://perqed.com/blog/torus-decomposition/
If anyone has a few minutes to look at the repository, I would massively appreciate any advice or feedback on how to write these proofs more idiomatically. Thank you!
Just wondering, is the blog written by hand or via AI? I know you mentioned AI was part of your coding process.

Apologies; I will remove it, but the intent was not a solicitation. It was just an explanation of why the link was to GitHub.

Yan Yablonovskiy 🇺🇦 said:

Just wondering, is the blog written by hand or via AI? I know you mentioned AI was part of your coding process.

Yes. This is the first proof-of-concept for what I hope will become an open source proof engine leveraging mostly open weight LLM models. The entire pipeline (from selecting a problem, developing the proof plan, drafting the paper, etc) is intended to be AI-first but with high observability so that a human can be in-the-loop. This includes drafting the blog and website, but with heavy editing since this was the first real example.
